These are the two sides of one distinction: --watch watches imported modules, --watch-path turns that off. sr13-06's statement ('keeps dependency watching enabled') already takes it as given that plain --watch watches dependencies, which is sr13-05's answer. sr13-05 is the weaker card because common sense alone guesses it.

sr5-04 says a string "exports" maps to the package's "." entry, which takes it as given that "." is the bare-package root entry, the whole of sr5-03. Knowing sr5-04 therefore answers sr5-03. sr5-03 is close to a definition card.

conflictGroups.name: threadpool-crypto
conflictGroups.why: sr1-12's statement says a slow crypto task runs in libuv's threadpool, which gives away that async pbkdf2() does not compute on the event loop thread (sr1-07).

conflictGroups.name: threadpool-vs-main-thread-mirror
conflictGroups.why: Mirrored false pair. sr1-03 and sr1-11 wrongly move event-loop work (network I/O, JSON.parse) to the threadpool, and sr1-07 wrongly moves threadpool work (pbkdf2) onto the event loop thread. Dealt together, they show the trick.

conflictGroups.name: threadpool-users
conflictGroups.why: Same true template ('async X uses libuv's threadpool'). sr1-12's explanation ('unrelated operations sharing the pool') primes a True answer for each of the others.

conflictGroups.name: js-single-thread
conflictGroups.why: sr1-01 states that one thread runs the JavaScript callbacks, which strongly hints that JSON.parse is not moved to the Worker Pool (sr1-11).

conflictGroups.name: dns-lookup-vs-resolve
conflictGroups.why: Two sides of the dns.lookup()/dns.resolve*() split. Once a card says lookup uses getaddrinfo (the call that reads /etc/hosts), the resolve4 card that contrasts with it is easy.

conflictGroups.name: poll-check-timer-order
conflictGroups.why: sr2-01's explanation (timers run after poll) plus sr2-07 (check runs immediates) and sr2-06 (immediates end the poll wait) give the order poll, then check, then timers, which answers sr3-09 (setImmediate runs first inside an I/O callback).

conflictGroups.name: immediate-check-phase
conflictGroups.why: sr2-07 says check runs 'each callback scheduled by setImmediate()', which steers the player on sr3-04 (a nested immediate deferred to the next iteration). Both cards cover how the check phase drains its queue.

conflictGroups.name: timer-ref
conflictGroups.why: sr2-11's explanation (unref controls keep-alive) gives away sr2-12, and both tie to sr2-10's exit-when-empty rule.

conflictGroups.name: next-tick-queue
conflictGroups.why: sr3-01's explanation (the next tick queue is outside the phases) and sr3-02 (it drains after the current operation) together answer sr3-07 (recursive nextTick starves poll).

conflictGroups.name: timeout-vs-immediate-order
conflictGroups.why: Two contexts of one distinction. sr3-09's 'Inside an I/O callback' qualifier and sr3-08's explanation ('depends on runtime timing') each tell the player the answer of the other card.

conflictGroups.name: emit-synchronous
conflictGroups.why: sr7-02's explanation (emit() synchronously calls listeners) gives away sr3-11: a listener attached after the constructor misses a synchronous emit.

conflictGroups.name: listener-order
conflictGroups.why: sr7-05 (prependListener puts later prepends first) presupposes that on() appends in registration order, which is sr7-02's answer.

conflictGroups.name: mjs-format
conflictGroups.why: sr4-10 treats a .mjs file as an ES module that a .cjs file requires, which hints sr4-01 (.mjs is always ESM).

conflictGroups.name: require-esm
conflictGroups.why: Both cards test require() of an ES module from a .cjs file. sr4-10's synchronous namespace return sits next to sr4-09's top-level await failure.

conflictGroups.name: exports-precedence-encapsulation
conflictGroups.why: sr5-02's explanation (unlisted subpaths are rejected) and sr5-12 (self-references go through "exports") both present "exports" as authoritative, which hints that it beats "main" (sr5-01).

conflictGroups.name: exports-dot-entry
conflictGroups.why: sr5-04's statement and both explanations define "." as the root entry, so each card gives away the other.

conflictGroups.name: package-imports-field
conflictGroups.why: Both cards test the "imports" field. sr5-10's explanation calls '#' specifiers 'private', which skews sr5-11's answer and puts the two next to each other.

conflictGroups.name: fs-recursive-option
conflictGroups.why: sr6-05 (rm needs recursive: true for a tree) and sr6-08's explanation (cp needs recursive: true) hint at each other. All three use the same recursive-option frame.

conflictGroups.name: path-join-resolve
conflictGroups.why: Two sides of the join/resolve distinction. sr6-10 shows that resolve builds absolute paths, which hints that join does not use the cwd (sr6-09).

conflictGroups.name: emitter-error-handling
conflictGroups.why: sr7-08's explanation ('handling them needs an error listener') and statement ('otherwise unhandled') hint that an unhandled 'error' throws (sr7-07). sr7-12's explanation routes rejections to 'error'.

conflictGroups.name: emitter-warning-vs-throw-mirror
conflictGroups.why: Mirrored false pair. sr7-07 gives the 'error' event the listener limit's behaviour (a warning), and sr7-09 gives the listener limit a hard-failure behaviour. sr7-09's explanation also names MaxListenersExceededWarning.

conflictGroups.name: buffer-shared-memory
conflictGroups.why: Same false template ('makes an independent copy' / 'keeps its own storage') on the same fact family (Buffer views share memory). Either explanation answers the other card.

conflictGroups.name: worker-process-scope
conflictGroups.why: Both cards turn on process.* calls being thread-local in a Worker. sr10-12's explanation (signal handling belongs to the main thread) hints sr10-11.

conflictGroups.name: env-inheritance
conflictGroups.why: sr10-10's explanation (the Worker copies the parent's environment) sits next to child_process options.env replacement. Dealt together, the cards are easy to compare or confuse.

conflictGroups.name: signal-listeners
conflictGroups.why: sr12-11's explanation ('the listener defines the response') and sr12-12's explanation (SIGKILL listener rejected) cover the same process.on(signal) rules. Read together, they settle sr10-12's main-thread-only point.

conflictGroups.name: unhandled-rejection-escalation
conflictGroups.why: sr11-04's statement (throw mode escalates), sr11-09's 'escalated promise rejection' and sr11-03's explanation (throw mode emits 'unhandledRejection' first) each hint the others' answers. sr11-05's explanation names the mode independence.

conflictGroups.name: uncaught-exception-last-resort
conflictGroups.why: sr11-06's explanation (last-resort cleanup before shutdown) and sr11-11's explanation (an external monitor restarts the app) come from the same docs warning, so each answers the other. sr11-08 is in the same paragraph.

conflictGroups.name: env-file-precedence
conflictGroups.why: sr12-04's explanation is scoped 'for variables supplied by environment files', which hints that environment values win (sr12-03). Both are precedence rules for --env-file.

conflictGroups.name: argv-vs-execargv
conflictGroups.why: Two sides of the argv/execArgv split. sr12-06's explanation lays out argv[0] and argv[1], and sr12-07's explanation says execArgv excludes script arguments.

conflictGroups.name: process-exit-events
conflictGroups.why: sr12-08's explanation (process.exit() forces termination) gives away sr12-09 (no 'beforeExit') and supports sr12-10 (async work in 'exit' is abandoned).

conflictGroups.name: node-test-outcome
conflictGroups.why: sr13-01's explanation (node:test waits for the returned promise) and sr13-02's (callback plus promise fails) describe the same pass/fail rules for one test function.

conflictGroups.name: watch-dependencies
conflictGroups.why: sr13-06's statement and explanation say --watch tracks imported modules, which is sr13-05's answer.

conflictGroups.name: type-stripping-erasable
conflictGroups.why: sr13-07's explanation ('strips erasable annotations') hints that enums, which need code generation, are rejected (sr13-09). sr13-10's explanation repeats the idea that only erasable or explicit type syntax is removed.

conflictGroups.name: release-phase-contents
conflictGroups.why: Their explanations describe each phase's intake: Current takes most nonbreaking changes, LTS features are selected, Maintenance takes critical fixes. Read together, they give each other away.

conflictGroups.name: lts-odd-even
conflictGroups.why: sr14-09's explanation ('promotes odd-numbered lines to LTS too') gives away sr14-07. sr14-07's 'Up to Node.js 26' scoping hints that the rule changes from 27.

conflictGroups.name: alpha-channel
conflictGroups.why: sr14-10's explanation ('compatibility testing') hints sr14-11 (Alpha is tested, unlike Nightly). sr14-12's explanation places Alpha before Current.

conflictGroups.why: sr14-04 says production should use only Active or Maintenance LTS, which hints that EOL lines get no fixes (sr14-05).

rewrite.reason: ambiguous: 'Node.js runs JavaScript callbacks on one event loop thread' reads as a whole-process claim that Workers contradict. Scoped to the main thread; the explanation now adds context from the guide.
rewrite.statement: The main thread of a Node.js process runs JavaScript callbacks on one event loop.
rewrite.explanation: The Don't Block guide says Node.js runs JavaScript initialization and callbacks on one Event Loop, also called the main thread, beside a Worker Pool of k threads.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Don't Block the Event Loop — callback execution

rewrite.reason: source_problem: the pinned nodejs.org page is available, so the GitHub doc/api citation breaks the source rule. URL swapped; card text unchanged.
rewrite.statement: fs.readFile() with a callback uses libuv's threadpool for its file operations.
rewrite.explanation: libuv workers perform the file operations used by asynchronous fs.readFile().

rewrite.reason: source_problem: the pinned nodejs.org page is available, so the GitHub doc/api citation breaks the source rule. URL swapped; card text unchanged.
rewrite.statement: crypto.pbkdf2() with a callback computes its result on the event loop thread.
rewrite.explanation: The asynchronous crypto.pbkdf2() computation runs in libuv's threadpool.
rewrite.misconception: The event loop performs the asynchronous key-derivation computation.

rewrite.reason: source_problem: the pinned nodejs.org page is available, so the GitHub doc/api citation breaks the source rule. URL swapped; card text unchanged.
rewrite.statement: Asynchronous zlib compression uses libuv's threadpool to perform the compression work.
rewrite.explanation: libuv workers execute zlib operations submitted by the asynchronous API.

rewrite.reason: source_problem: GitHub cli.md swapped for the pinned cli.html. The explanation now gives the reason and the remedy, using the docs' 'not guaranteed to work ... created ... before user code is run'.
rewrite.statement: Assigning process.env.UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE in user code reliably resizes libuv's threadpool.
rewrite.explanation: Setting it from inside the process is not guaranteed to work, because the runtime creates the threadpool before user code runs; set UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE in the environment when starting node.
rewrite.misconception: Changing the environment variable during execution reliably changes the pool.

rewrite.reason: source_problem plus tell: GitHub cli.md swapped for cli.html. The statement drops the restriction word 'just' (scan pattern 4) and keeps the same fact and answer (false). The explanation now names the cause ('fixed size', 'seemingly unrelated') without listing which APIs use the pool.
rewrite.statement: Node.js confines the slowdown from a long crypto task in libuv's threadpool to other crypto calls.
rewrite.explanation: Because libuv's threadpool has a fixed size, a slow task in it degrades the performance of other, seemingly unrelated APIs that also run in the pool.
rewrite.misconception: A slow threadpool task only affects other tasks of the same kind.

rewrite.reason: weak_card (LIFO strawman), rewritten instead of dropped because dropping sr2-02, 03, 10 and 12 would leave r2 with 8 cards. Verifier replacement, confirmed in the Learn guide: 'execute callbacks in that phase's queue until the queue has been exhausted or the maximum number of callbacks has executed'.
rewrite.statement: The event loop runs one callback from a phase's queue, then moves on to the next phase.
rewrite.explanation: Each phase has a FIFO queue; the event loop runs its callbacks until the queue is exhausted or a maximum number has run, then moves to the next phase.
rewrite.misconception: The event loop takes a single callback from each phase per iteration, round-robin.
rewrite.sourceTitle: The Node.js Event Loop — event loop explained

rewrite.reason: tell: drops the persistence verb 'keeps' (scan pattern 2) and makes the event loop the actor, as the verifier suggested. Same fact, still false. Guide: 'if a callback has been scheduled with setImmediate() and the poll phase becomes idle, it will end ... rather than waiting'.
rewrite.statement: With setImmediate() callbacks queued, the event loop waits in the poll phase for new I/O.
rewrite.explanation: With immediates queued, the event loop ends the poll phase rather than waiting for new I/O.
rewrite.misconception: Pending immediates leave poll's I/O wait unchanged.

rewrite.reason: ambiguous plus GitHub source: 'schedules its callback for the exact instant' mixed due time with run time. The statement now claims the run time. The source is timers.html: 'The callback will likely not be invoked in precisely delay milliseconds ... no guarantees about the exact timing ... as close as possible'.
rewrite.statement: A setTimeout() callback runs exactly delay milliseconds after the setTimeout() call.
rewrite.explanation: The timers docs say the callback will likely not run in precisely delay milliseconds; Node.js calls it as close as possible to that time and makes no guarantee about exact timing.
rewrite.misconception: A timer delay guarantees an exact execution time.

rewrite.reason: source_problem: GitHub timers.md swapped for timers.html#timeoutunref. The explanation now says what unref() changes ('will not require the Node.js event loop to remain active').
rewrite.statement: timeout.unref() cancels the timeout's scheduled callback.
rewrite.explanation: unref() only stops the timer from keeping the process alive; if other activity keeps the event loop running, the callback still runs.
rewrite.misconception: Removing a timer's reference cancels its work.

rewrite.reason: ambiguous: a nextTick queued from an I/O callback does run while the loop is in poll, and the card overlapped sr3-02. Replaced with the verifier's card on the section's untested Learn naming remark. Guide text confirmed: 'process.nextTick() fires immediately on the same phase; setImmediate() fires on the following iteration ... the names should be swapped'.
rewrite.statement: The Learn event loop guide says process.nextTick() fires on a later loop iteration than setImmediate().
rewrite.explanation: The guide says process.nextTick() fires immediately on the same phase while setImmediate() fires on the following iteration, so in essence the names should be swapped.
rewrite.misconception: process.nextTick() runs on the next loop iteration, as its name suggests.
rewrite.sourceTitle: The Node.js Event Loop — process.nextTick() vs setImmediate()

rewrite.reason: source_problem: the pinned nodejs.org timers page is available (same sentence: 'will not be triggered until the next event loop iteration'). URL swapped; card text unchanged.
rewrite.statement: A setImmediate() callback queued inside another immediate runs in the same event loop iteration.
rewrite.explanation: Node.js defers the nested immediate to the next iteration.
rewrite.misconception: An executing immediate's new immediate joins the current iteration.

rewrite.reason: source_problem: the cited Understanding setImmediate() page does not support the main-module scope and uses 'macrotask' wording. The event loop guide says 'not within an I/O cycle (i.e. the main module), the order ... is non-deterministic'.
rewrite.statement: The main CommonJS module gives setTimeout(fn, 0) callbacks priority over setImmediate(fn) callbacks.
rewrite.explanation: Their order in the main CommonJS module depends on runtime timing.
rewrite.misconception: A zero-delay timeout has a fixed scheduling priority in the main module.
rewrite.sourceTitle: The Node.js Event Loop — setImmediate() vs setTimeout()

rewrite.reason: source_problem: the pinned nodejs.org timers page is available ('value <any> A value with which the promise is fulfilled'). URL swapped; card text unchanged.
rewrite.statement: setTimeout() from node:timers/promises fulfills its promise with the supplied value.
rewrite.explanation: The optional value becomes the promise's fulfillment result.

rewrite.reason: source_problem: the pinned nodejs.org timers page is available ('When canceled, the returned Promises will be rejected with an AbortError'). URL swapped; card text unchanged.
rewrite.statement: Aborting a pending node:timers/promises timeout via its supplied signal fulfills the promise early.
rewrite.explanation: Cancelling with AbortSignal rejects the timer promise with AbortError.
rewrite.misconception: Cancelling a promise timer counts as successful early completion.

rewrite.statement: By default, Node.js loads a .mjs file as an ES module in a package with "type": "commonjs".
rewrite.explanation: The .mjs extension determines the file's module format.
